title: A Systematic Review of Optimization Algorithms for Structural Health Monitoring and Optimal Sensor Placement

subsections.subsection_title: Integration of Machine Learning and Data-Driven Approaches in SHM
subsections.content:
The integration of machine learning (ML) and data-driven approaches has revolutionized Structural Health Monitoring (SHM) by enabling automated, adaptive, and high-accuracy damage detection without relying solely on physics-based models. Deep learning architectures, particularly deep neural networks, have demonstrated exceptional capability in extracting hierarchical features from complex vibration and strain data, facilitating robust classification of structural anomalies even under noisy conditions ref [2]. Recent studies have combined deep stacked autoencoders with optimization algorithms to enhance diagnostic accuracy in concrete structures, leveraging multi-sensor fusion and dimensionality reduction techniques to improve reliability under limited sensor configurations ref [3]. Furthermore, unsupervised learning methods have proven effective in detecting unknown damage patterns in real-world steel bridges, achieving performance comparable to supervised approaches by identifying deviations from normal operational baselines ref [18]. The application of rare event modeling through Extreme Function Theory (EFT) has also emerged as a statistically rigorous framework for detecting infrequent damage events by modeling deviations in mode shapes as extreme deviations from normal distributions ref [12].

Beyond damage identification, ML is increasingly employed to optimize sensor placement by learning latent relationships between sensor data and system states. For instance, deep neural networks have been successfully applied to determine optimal sensor configurations in turbulent flow systems, demonstrating how data-driven surrogate models can reduce computational cost while preserving reconstruction fidelity in data assimilation tasks ref [10]. These advances underscore a paradigm shift in SHM: from model-dependent, rule-based diagnostics to data-centric, learning-driven frameworks that adapt to structural complexity and environmental variability. The synergy between ML, sensor fusion, and statistical learning is now central to developing scalable, real-time SHM systems for critical infrastructure.

subsections.subsection_title: Structural Health Monitoring: Methods and Sensor Technologies
subsections.content:
Structural Health Monitoring (SHM) relies on a diverse array of sensing technologies and non-destructive testing (NDT) methods to detect, localize, and characterize damage in structural systems. Strain sensing remains a cornerstone of SHM, with electrical and fiber-optic sensors—particularly fiber Bragg grating (FBG) systems—established as mature technologies for both discrete and distributed strain measurement across civil infrastructure, as detailed in the century-long evolution of strain sensors ref [9]. Beyond strain, ultrasonic techniques have gained prominence, especially in complex systems like railway tracks, where diffuse ultrasonic waves (DUW) combined with PZT/FBG hybrid systems enable sensitive detection of incipient damage through waveform distortion metrics ref [10]. In composite materials, where damage modes such as delamination and fiber breakage are often internal and invisible, electromagnetic wave NDT (EMW-NDT) has emerged as a promising method, demonstrating high sensitivity to delamination size and thickness in CFRP composites ref [11]. Acoustic emission (AE) tomography, integrated with advanced inversion algorithms like L-BFGS, offers real-time cavity damage detection in automated machinery, overcoming limitations of conventional AE methods ref [12].

The breadth of SHM methodologies is further illustrated by systematic reviews covering wind turbine monitoring, which survey visual, infrared, ultrasonic, and electromagnetic techniques applied via human, robotic, or UAV platforms ref [14], and image-based SHM, which leverages computer vision for automated defect identification, 3D modeling, and large-scale infrastructure monitoring ref [15]. A comprehensive review of SHM in composite structures highlights the integration of vibration-based methods with advanced signal processing and machine learning to address nonlinear damage modes ref [13], while a broader NDT review contextualizes these techniques within industrial quality assurance frameworks ref [9]. Together, these advances reflect a paradigm shift from localized, manual inspections to distributed, automated, and data-rich monitoring systems that enhance safety, reduce maintenance costs, and enable predictive infrastructure management.

subsections.subsection_title: Optimal Sensor Placement: Theory and Methodologies
subsections.content:
Optimal sensor placement (OSP) in structural health monitoring (SHM) seeks to identify the minimal set of sensor locations that maximizes the information content for modal identification, damage detection, and system identification. Classical methodologies include the Effective Independence (EI) method, which iteratively removes candidate sensors that contribute least to the linear independence of mode shapes, thereby maximizing the determinant of the Fisher information matrix ref [18]. The Modal Kinetic Energy (MKE) method, which selects sensors at locations of high modal energy, has been shown to be a non-iterative precursor to EI, with the latter refining the selection through repeated ortho-normalization of reduced mode shapes ref [20]. Recent theoretical advances have unified these approaches under information-theoretic frameworks, where sensor configurations are optimized to minimize the condition number and maximize the trace of the Fisher matrix, ensuring robust parameter estimation ref [18], ref [21].

To address structural uncertainties, non-probabilistic approaches have emerged, particularly the interval effective independence method, which extends EI to interval-valued Fisher matrices using interval analysis, enabling robust sensor selection under bounded parameter uncertainties ref [19]. Further innovations include the RISEN index, which jointly optimizes sensor number and location via multi-objective evolutionary algorithms, integrating interval-based EI and eigenvalue vector product objectives ref [12]. In bridge systems, frameworks combining EI, EI-DPR, KE, and modified variance (MV) methods—validated via Modal Assurance Criterion (MAC)—have demonstrated efficacy in balancing cost and accuracy ref [9]. For mid-frequency regimes where modal density complicates traditional methods, frequency-domain approaches using principal components of frequency response functions (FEfi) offer a viable alternative to mode-shape-based techniques ref [20]. An overview of combinatorial, neural network, and information-theoretic methods highlights the versatility of OSP across sensor types and structural systems ref [18].

subsections.subsection_title: Optimization Algorithms for Sensor Placement and Damage Identification
subsections.content:
Optimization algorithms play a pivotal role in simultaneously addressing sensor placement and damage identification in structural health monitoring (SHM), where the dual objectives of maximizing information content and minimizing computational cost are often conflicting. Differential evolution (DE) has emerged as a dominant meta-heuristic in this domain, with multiple variants demonstrating superior performance in detecting multi-damage scenarios in truss and plate-like structures. For instance, ref [27] employed DE with vibration-based objective functions to accurately localize and quantify damage in planar and space trusses, outperforming genetic algorithms. Subsequent advancements introduced accelerated DE variants with novel mutation and exchange operators to enhance convergence speed and avoid premature convergence, as demonstrated in ref [8] for plate structures. Furthermore, hybrid approaches such as the adaptive sine cosine algorithm integrated with DE (ASCA-DE) have shown improved robustness in complex damage detection problems by leveraging the exploration capabilities of both algorithms, as shown in ref [28].

Beyond DE, simulated annealing (SA) has been adapted for optimal sensor placement through improved sampling strategies and coordinate-based search spaces, reducing computational burden while maintaining solution quality, as evidenced in ref [16]. Comparative studies between SA and genetic algorithm frameworks, such as in ref [17], reveal trade-offs between accuracy and computational efficiency, with GA-EnKF achieving higher precision but SA-EnKF offering lower computational cost. Additionally, the application of tabu search methods, such as the modified continuous reactive tabu search (MCRTS) in ref [19], enables the identification of multiple local optima in multi-modal damage scenarios, particularly in beam structures where frequency-based indicators are ambiguous. The adaptability of DE has also extended beyond structural systems, with ref [10] demonstrating its efficacy in 3D directional wireless sensor network deployment, highlighting its potential for spatially distributed SHM architectures. These algorithmic innovations collectively underscore the growing synergy between optimization theory and SHM practice.

subsections.subsection_title: Multi-Objective and Adaptive Optimization for SHM Sensor Layouts
subsections.content:
Multi-objective optimization has emerged as a critical paradigm in structural health monitoring (SHM) sensor layout design, where conflicting criteria—such as coverage, redundancy, cost, and robustness to noise—must be simultaneously balanced. Adaptive optimization frameworks further enhance this by dynamically adjusting search strategies based on real-time feedback from structural response data, improving convergence and resilience to model uncertainties. Ref [1] demonstrates a neural network-based sensitivity analysis to optimize multi-sensor geometries by identifying redundant channels, effectively reducing sensor count while preserving diagnostic fidelity. Similarly, ref [5] introduces a Bayesian risk minimization framework that adaptively weights detection errors (Type I/II) to determine optimal actuator-sensor configurations under non-uniform damage probabilities, validated through guided ultrasonic wave simulations. These approaches align with the broader trend of integrating probabilistic decision theory into sensor placement, as seen in ref [7], where combinatorial optimization of sensor/actuator locations for active acoustic control leverages experimental data to balance performance and physical constraints. Adaptive algorithms, including genetic algorithms with time-varying mutation rates, enable dynamic reconfiguration in response to evolving structural conditions, making them particularly suited for large-scale or non-stationary systems.

Recent advances have extended these principles to hybrid multi-objective formulations that incorporate entropy-based information metrics, modal kinetic energy, and computational efficiency as competing objectives. Such formulations are often solved using Pareto-optimal evolutionary strategies, allowing engineers to select trade-off solutions based on operational priorities. The integration of adaptive learning mechanisms, such as online sensitivity recalibration and Bayesian updating, further refines placement strategies in real-time monitoring scenarios, reducing reliance on static pre-deployment models.

subsections.subsection_title: Discrete and Mixed-Integer Optimization Methods for Sensor Networks
subsections.content:
Discrete and mixed-integer optimization methods are essential for structural health monitoring (SHM) sensor network design, where sensor locations must be selected from a finite set of candidate positions, often subject to budgetary, topological, or connectivity constraints. These problems are inherently combinatorial and NP-hard, necessitating specialized algorithms that handle integer decision variables and discrete feasibility spaces. The discrete monkey algorithm (DMA), originally developed for transmission network expansion, has been adapted to SHM contexts to efficiently navigate large discrete solution spaces with small population sizes, demonstrating robustness in high-dimensional sensor layout problems ref [32]. Mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) formulations have also been employed to optimize sensor placements under modal observability and redundancy constraints, leveraging commercial solvers for exact solutions in small-to-medium structures. Tabu search and simulated annealing variants have been successfully applied to enforce discrete sensor counts while maximizing modal energy coverage, outperforming continuous relaxations in practical deployments. Recent work has integrated binary encoding with evolutionary operators to preserve feasibility, enabling scalable solutions for complex civil infrastructure networks.

Hybrid approaches combining MILP with metaheuristics have emerged to balance solution accuracy and computational tractability, particularly for large-scale bridges and aerospace structures. These methods often decompose the problem into continuous subproblems for response sensitivity estimation and discrete subproblems for sensor selection, iteratively refining the layout. The use of constraint programming and branch-and-bound techniques has further improved convergence in multi-objective discrete settings, where trade-offs between cost, coverage, and robustness are critical. While most applications remain in the domain of power systems and mechanical networks, the transferability of these methods to SHM is gaining traction, especially with the increasing availability of high-fidelity finite element models and real-time data streams.

subsections.subsection_title: Hybrid and Quantum-Inspired Optimization for SHM
subsections.content: Hybrid and quantum-inspired optimization methods have emerged as powerful paradigms for addressing the combinatorial complexity of optimal sensor placement in structural health monitoring (SHM). By integrating evolutionary strategies with gradient-based techniques, hybrid algorithms such as GENOUD combine global search robustness with local convergence efficiency, enabling effective navigation of non-convex, discontinuous objective landscapes common in sensor layout problems ref [33]. These approaches mitigate the risk of premature convergence inherent in pure evolutionary methods while avoiding the local optima traps of classical gradient descent. Concurrently, quantum-inspired optimization leverages principles from quantum computing—such as superposition and entanglement—to explore solution spaces more efficiently than classical counterparts. Recent advances in quantum second-order optimization algorithms, capable of handling general polynomials with poly(log d) complexity, offer promising avenues for accelerating the evaluation of sensor placement metrics based on modal observability and information entropy ref [34]. Although direct quantum hardware implementations remain nascent in SHM, classical simulations of quantum annealing and variational quantum circuits have demonstrated superior exploration capabilities in high-dimensional discrete spaces, particularly for mixed-integer sensor network design. These hybrid and quantum-inspired frameworks are increasingly being adapted to multi-objective SHM criteria, balancing coverage, cost, and robustness under uncertainty.

subsections.subsection_title: Derivative-Free Optimization Algorithms for Sensor Placement
subsections.content:
Derivative-free optimization (DFO) algorithms have gained increasing traction in structural health monitoring (SHM) sensor placement due to their ability to optimize complex, non-differentiable, and computationally expensive objective functions without requiring gradient information. These methods are particularly suited for SHM applications where the objective function—often based on modal observability, strain energy distribution, or information-theoretic metrics—is evaluated via finite element simulations or experimental data, rendering analytical derivatives infeasible. Direct search methods, such as pattern search and Nelder-Mead, along with surrogate-based approaches like kriging and radial basis functions, have been successfully applied to discrete sensor placement problems, balancing coverage, redundancy, and cost constraints. Ref. [1] provides a comprehensive review and empirical comparison of 22 DFO solvers, identifying TOMLAB/MULTI-MIN, MCS, and TOMLAB/LGO as top performers in global optimization under limited function evaluations, making them strong candidates for large-scale SHM networks. Recent studies have integrated DFO with information-theoretic criteria such as entropy and Fisher information to enhance spatial coverage and robustness to model uncertainty.

Hybrid DFO frameworks combining local refinement with global exploration have demonstrated improved convergence in high-dimensional sensor layout problems. For instance, surrogate-assisted evolutionary DFO has been employed to optimize sensor configurations in bridge and aerospace structures, reducing computational burden while maintaining solution quality. The robustness of DFO to noise and discontinuities also makes it suitable for real-time or field-deployed SHM systems where sensor responses may be corrupted by environmental variability. While DFO methods are less commonly applied than evolutionary or gradient-based techniques in SHM literature, their theoretical grounding and empirical performance in benchmark optimization tasks underscore their underutilized potential for optimal sensor network design.

subsections.subsection_title: Evolutionary Algorithms in Optimal Sensor Placement
subsections.content:
Evolutionary algorithms (EAs) have emerged as powerful tools for optimal sensor placement in structural health monitoring (SHM), effectively navigating the combinatorial complexity of discrete sensor configurations. Genetic algorithms (GAs), a prominent subclass of EAs, have been widely adopted to maximize information content while minimizing sensor count. For instance, ref [36] introduced the Single Parenthood Genetic Algorithm (SPGA) integrated with the Modal Assurance Criterion (MAC), demonstrating superior search efficiency and reliability over conventional GA and step-accumulation methods in a 61-degree-of-freedom truss structure. Similarly, ref [37] proposed a Geometrical Viewpoint-based Genetic Algorithm (GVGA) that optimizes sensor layouts by minimizing noise sensitivity through a fitness function derived from elliptical noise diameters in response space, significantly enhancing convergence in space structures.

Recent advancements have extended EAs to multiobjective frameworks, addressing conflicting criteria such as modal identifiability, signal redundancy, and noise resilience. ref [5] developed a decomposition-based multiobjective evolutionary algorithm combined with particle swarm optimization to simultaneously optimize linear independence of mode shapes, dynamic redundancy, and vibration signal strength, achieving balanced trade-offs via a distance-based multiobjective decision-making strategy. These approaches highlight the shift from single-objective optimization toward holistic sensor layout design, improving robustness under real-world measurement uncertainties. The adaptability of EAs to nonlinear, non-convex objective landscapes makes them particularly suited for large-scale and complex structural systems where analytical gradients are intractable.

subsections.subsection_title: Evolutionary Algorithms for Sensor Placement Optimization
subsections.content:
Evolutionary algorithms (EAs) have emerged as powerful tools for optimizing sensor placement in structural health monitoring (SHM) due to their ability to navigate complex, non-convex search spaces and handle discrete, multi-objective formulations. Among these, genetic algorithms (GAs) have been widely adopted for their robustness in identifying optimal sensor configurations that maximize modal information while minimizing sensor count, as demonstrated in early applications to space structures and bridge systems. Ref [1] provides a foundational comparison between GA and particle swarm optimization (PSO), showing that while both are population-based, PSO often achieves comparable solution quality with fewer function evaluations, making it particularly attractive for computationally intensive SHM problems. Subsequent studies have extended these frameworks to include hybrid EAs, integrating local search heuristics to refine convergence and avoid premature stagnation. Differential evolution (DE) variants have also been applied to sensor placement, leveraging mutation and crossover operators to explore high-dimensional design spaces efficiently, especially in large-scale truss and plate-like structures. Multi-objective EAs, such as NSGA-II and MOEA/D, have further enabled simultaneous optimization of criteria like observability, redundancy, and cost, yielding Pareto-optimal sensor layouts that balance competing performance metrics.

Recent advances have incorporated machine learning surrogates to reduce the computational burden of finite element evaluations during EA iterations, enabling real-time or near-real-time sensor optimization in dynamic environments. The adaptability of EAs to varying structural topologies and boundary conditions has solidified their role as a standard approach in SHM, particularly where analytical methods fail due to nonlinearity or uncertainty. Ongoing research continues to explore hybridizations with swarm intelligence and memetic strategies to enhance exploration-exploitation trade-offs, ensuring scalable and reliable sensor network design across diverse civil and aerospace infrastructure.

subsections.subsection_title: Simulated Annealing for Multiobjective Sensor Optimization
subsections.content:
Simulated Annealing (SA) has been effectively adapted for multiobjective sensor placement optimization in structural health monitoring (SHM), offering a robust alternative to evolutionary approaches by mimicking thermodynamic annealing processes to escape local optima. The AMOSA algorithm, introduced by Bandyopadhyay et al., integrates an archive mechanism to preserve non-dominated solutions and employs a domination-based acceptance probability that considers both current and archived solutions, significantly enhancing convergence in high-dimensional objective spaces ref [40]. This method has demonstrated superior performance over traditional MOEAs in problems with four or more objectives, making it particularly suitable for complex SHM systems requiring simultaneous optimization of coverage, redundancy, and cost. Subsequent studies have extended AMOSA to incorporate clustering techniques for maintaining solution diversity and reducing computational overhead, further improving its applicability to large-scale structures ref [40]. Other SA-based variants have been proposed to handle discrete sensor location constraints, integrating modal information and effective independence metrics to guide the search toward optimal configurations ref [10]. Comparative analyses have shown that SA-based multiobjective frameworks often outperform genetic algorithms in convergence stability and solution uniformity, especially under noisy or incomplete modal data conditions ref [14].

Recent applications have coupled SA with surrogate models and machine learning to accelerate evaluation of sensor configurations, reducing the computational burden of finite element simulations. Hybrid SA-decomposition strategies have also emerged, enabling parallel exploration of multiple objective trade-offs while preserving the algorithm’s probabilistic acceptance criterion. These advancements underscore SA’s adaptability in multiobjective SHM contexts, where balancing conflicting criteria—such as sensor count, spatial coverage, and robustness to noise—is critical. While less prevalent than evolutionary methods, SA-based approaches offer distinct advantages in exploration efficiency and parameter sensitivity, particularly when the search space is rugged or discontinuous.

subsections.subsection_title: Performance Comparison of Optimization Algorithms in Structural Design
subsections.content:
The performance of optimization algorithms in structural design has been extensively compared to identify the most effective approaches for weight reduction, stiffness maximization, and constraint satisfaction. Yildiz [2] conducted a comprehensive evaluation of six population-based algorithms—including genetic algorithm, particle swarm optimization, immune algorithm, artificial bee colony, and differential evolution—demonstrating that a hybrid differential evolution approach achieved a 28.4% volume reduction in a vehicle component, outperforming all standalone methods. Similar comparative studies have validated the superiority of hybrid and adaptive variants over conventional evolutionary techniques, particularly in high-dimensional, nonlinear design spaces. For instance, ref [21] showed that differential evolution outperformed other metaheuristics in 3D wireless sensor network deployment, a problem structurally analogous to sensor placement optimization. Other works have benchmarked simulated annealing against evolutionary strategies in structural weight minimization, revealing trade-offs between convergence speed and global optimality. Recent comparisons also include memetic algorithms and quantum-inspired optimizers, which exhibit enhanced exploration capabilities in complex structural systems. The Taguchi method, employed in conjunction with evolutionary algorithms, has further improved robustness in parameter tuning, as demonstrated in welded beam and truss design problems.

Notably, the choice of algorithm often depends on problem characteristics: discrete problems favor genetic algorithms, while continuous problems benefit from differential evolution. However, hybridization remains a dominant trend, as single-algorithm approaches frequently struggle with premature convergence or local optima trapping. These findings underscore the importance of algorithm selection and hybridization in structural design optimization, with implications for sensor placement where computational efficiency and solution quality are equally critical.

Table 7 synthesizes optimization algorithms applied to optimal sensor placement (OSP) in structural health monitoring (SHM), highlighting their performance metrics, computational efficiency, and suitability for complex structural systems. Evolutionary algorithms such as differential evolution have demonstrated robustness in multi-objective OSP problems, particularly in large-scale truss and plate-like structures [11], while modified simulated annealing variants improve convergence in modal identification tasks [32]. Multi-objective decomposition-based frameworks, including those integrating NSGA-II and MOEA/D, have been shown to balance coverage, redundancy, and cost constraints effectively [6]. Recent advances incorporate hybrid metaheuristics, such as adaptive sine cosine algorithms fused with differential evolution, to enhance exploration-exploitation trade-offs in damage-sensitive sensor layouts [9]. Non-probabilistic approaches, including interval-based effective independence methods, offer viable alternatives under uncertainty without assuming statistical distributions [13]. Additionally, derivative-free optimization techniques have gained traction for their applicability in high-dimensional, non-differentiable objective spaces common in SHM [21]. Neural network-driven sensitivity measures have also been employed to guide sensor placement by quantifying output responsiveness to structural changes [36]. The integration of quantum-inspired optimization and swarm intelligence, such as the discrete monkey algorithm, remains underexplored but shows promise for combinatorial OSP [24].

Comparative studies reveal that while genetic algorithms remain popular for their interpretability, their convergence speed is often outperformed by particle swarm and ant colony variants in dynamic environments [2]. Recent work has also emphasized the importance of algorithm selection based on structural topology, with population-based methods excelling in spatially distributed systems and gradient-free methods preferred for sensor count minimization [30]. The growing adoption of data-driven surrogate models further reduces computational burden, enabling real-time OSP in large infrastructure networks [20].

Optimization algorithms for structural health monitoring (SHM) have increasingly leveraged metaheuristic and hybrid approaches to address the combinatorial complexity of sensor placement. Recent studies have demonstrated the efficacy of particle swarm optimization (PSO) variants in balancing coverage and redundancy, particularly in large-scale infrastructure [22]. The integration of machine learning with evolutionary algorithms has further enhanced adaptability, with neural network-driven sensitivity metrics guiding sensor selection in dynamic environments [19]. Multi-objective frameworks, such as those employing non-dominated sorting genetic algorithms (NSGA-II), have been successfully applied to simultaneously optimize modal observability and cost constraints [24]. Additionally, differential evolution (DE) has shown robust performance in high-dimensional spaces, especially when coupled with constraint-handling mechanisms for discrete sensor locations [37]. Hybrid strategies combining simulated annealing with local search heuristics have improved convergence speed while avoiding premature stagnation [25]. Recent work has also explored quantum-inspired optimization for polynomial-based objective functions in SHM, offering promising computational advantages [37]. The use of surrogate models, including Gaussian processes and deep neural networks, has reduced computational burden in iterative optimization loops [9]. Furthermore, non-probabilistic approaches based on interval analysis have been proposed to account for uncertainty in modal parameters without assuming statistical distributions [7].

Emerging trends include the application of swarm intelligence algorithms such as the firefly algorithm and cuckoo search, which have been adapted for sensor network topology optimization [28]. The effectiveness of these methods has been validated through both numerical simulations and experimental setups on bridge and aerospace structures [31]. Comparative analyses have highlighted the superiority of hybrid DE-PSO frameworks over single-algorithm approaches in terms of solution diversity and robustness [28]. The integration of real-time data assimilation with optimization has enabled adaptive sensor placement, particularly in systems with time-varying dynamics [9]. These advances collectively underscore a shift toward intelligent, data-driven, and multi-criteria optimization paradigms in SHM.
